12: /// A type that encapsulates "inner" literal extractiong from a regex.
13: ///
14: /// It uses a huge pile of heuristics to try to pluck out literals from a regex
15: /// that are in turn used to build a simpler regex that is more amenable to
16: /// optimization.
17: ///
18: /// The main idea underyling the validity of this technique is the fact
19: /// that ripgrep searches individuals lines and not across lines. (Unless
20: /// -U/--multiline is enabled.) Namely, we can pluck literals out of the regex,
21: /// search for them, find the bounds of the line in which that literal occurs
22: /// and then run the original regex on only that line. This overall works
23: /// really really well in throughput oriented searches because it potentially
24: /// allows ripgrep to spend a lot more time in a fast vectorized routine for
25: /// finding literals as opposed to the (much) slower regex engine.
26: ///
27: /// This optimization was far more important in the old days, but since then,
28: /// Rust's regex engine has actually grown its own (albeit limited) support for
29: /// inner literal optimizations. So this technique doesn't apply as much as it
30: /// used to.
31: ///
32: /// A good example of a regex where this particular extractor helps is
33: /// `\s+(Sherlock|[A-Z]atso[a-z]|Moriarty)\s+`. The `[A-Z]` before the `atso`
34: /// in particular is what inhibits the regex engine's own inner literal
35: /// optimizations from kicking in. This particular regex also did not have any
36: /// inner literals extracted in the old implementation (ripgrep <=13). So this
37: /// particular implementation represents a strict improvement from both the old
38: /// implementation and from the regex engine's own optimizations. (Which could
39: /// in theory be improved still.)
40: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
41: pub(crate) struct InnerLiterals {
42:     seq: Seq,
43: }
44: 
45: impl InnerLiterals {
46:     /// Create a set of inner literals from the given HIR expression.
47:     ///
48:     /// If no line terminator was configured, then this always declines to
49:     /// extract literals because the inner literal optimization may not be
50:     /// valid.
51:     ///
52:     /// Note that this requires the actual regex that will be used for a search
53:     /// because it will query some state about the compiled regex. That state
54:     /// may influence inner literal extraction.
55:     pub(crate) fn new(chir: &ConfiguredHIR, re: &Regex) -> InnerLiterals {
56:         // If there's no line terminator, then the inner literal optimization
57:         // at this level is not valid.
58:         if chir.config().line_terminator.is_none() {
59:             log::trace!(
60:                 "skipping inner literal extraction, \
61:                  no line terminator is set"
62:             );
63:             return InnerLiterals::none();
64:         }
65:         // If we believe the regex is already accelerated, then just let
66:         // the regex engine do its thing. We'll skip the inner literal
67:         // optimization.
68:         if re.is_accelerated() {
69:             log::trace!(
70:                 "skipping inner literal extraction, \
71:                  existing regex is believed to already be accelerated",
72:             );
73:             return InnerLiterals::none();
74:         }
75:         // In this case, we pretty much know that the regex engine will handle
76:         // it as best as possible, even if it isn't reported as accelerated.
77:         if chir.hir().properties().is_alternation_literal() {
78:             log::trace!(
79:                 "skipping inner literal extraction, \
80:                  found alternation of literals, deferring to regex engine",
81:             );
82:             return InnerLiterals::none();
83:         }
84:         let seq = Extractor::new().extract_untagged(chir.hir());
85:         InnerLiterals { seq }
86:     }
87: 
88:     /// Returns a infinite set of inner literals, such that it can never
89:     /// produce a matcher.
90:     pub(crate) fn none() -> InnerLiterals {
91:         InnerLiterals { seq: Seq::infinite() }
92:     }
93: 
94:     /// If it is deemed advantageous to do so (via various suspicious
95:     /// heuristics), this will return a single regular expression pattern that
96:     /// matches a subset of the language matched by the regular expression that
97:     /// generated these literal sets. The idea here is that the pattern
98:     /// returned by this method is much cheaper to search for. i.e., It is
99:     /// usually a single literal or an alternation of literals.
100:     pub(crate) fn one_regex(&self) -> Result<Option<Regex>, Error> {
101:         let Some(lits) = self.seq.literals() else { return Ok(None) };
102:         if lits.is_empty() {

106:         for lit in lits.iter() {
107:             alts.push(Hir::literal(lit.as_bytes()));
108:         }
109:         let hir = Hir::alternation(alts);
110:         log::debug!("extracted fast line regex: {:?}", hir.to_string());
111:         let re = Regex::builder()
112:             .configure(Regex::config().utf8_empty(false))
113:             .build_from_hir(&hir)
114:             .map_err(Error::regex)?;

116:     }

119: /// An inner literal extractor.
120: ///
121: /// This is a somewhat stripped down version of the extractor from
122: /// regex-syntax. The main difference is that we try to identify a "best" set
123: /// of required literals while traversing the HIR.
124: #[derive(Debug)]
125: struct Extractor {
126:     limit_class: usize,
127:     limit_repeat: usize,
128:     limit_literal_len: usize,
129:     limit_total: usize,
130: }
131: 
132: impl Extractor {
133:     /// Create a new inner literal extractor with a default configuration.
134:     fn new() -> Extractor {
135:         Extractor {
136:             limit_class: 10,
137:             limit_repeat: 10,
138:             limit_literal_len: 100,
139:             limit_total: 64,
140:         }
141:     }
142: 
143:     /// Execute the extractor at the top-level and return an untagged sequence
144:     /// of literals.
145:     fn extract_untagged(&self, hir: &Hir) -> Seq {
146:         let mut seq = self.extract(hir);
147:         log::trace!("extracted inner literals: {:?}", seq.seq);
148:         seq.seq.optimize_for_prefix_by_preference();
149:         log::trace!(
150:             "extracted inner literals after optimization: {:?}",
151:             seq.seq
152:         );
153:         if !seq.is_good() {
154:             log::trace!(
155:                 "throwing away inner literals because they might be slow"
156:             );
157:             seq.make_infinite();
158:         }
159:         seq.seq
160:     }
161: 
162:     /// Execute the extractor and return a sequence of literals.
163:     fn extract(&self, hir: &Hir) -> TSeq {
164:         use regex_syntax::hir::HirKind::*;
165: 
166:         match *hir.kind() {
167:             Empty | Look(_) => TSeq::singleton(self::Literal::exact(vec![])),
168:             Literal(hir::Literal(ref bytes)) => {
169:                 let mut seq =
170:                     TSeq::singleton(self::Literal::exact(bytes.to_vec()));
171:                 self.enforce_literal_len(&mut seq);
172:                 seq
173:             }
174:             Class(hir::Class::Unicode(ref cls)) => {
175:                 self.extract_class_unicode(cls)
176:             }
177:             Class(hir::Class::Bytes(ref cls)) => self.extract_class_bytes(cls),
178:             Repetition(ref rep) => self.extract_repetition(rep),
179:             Capture(hir::Capture { ref sub, .. }) => self.extract(sub),
180:             Concat(ref hirs) => self.extract_concat(hirs.iter()),
181:             Alternation(ref hirs) => self.extract_alternation(hirs.iter()),
182:         }
183:     }
184: 
185:     /// Extract a sequence from the given concatenation. Sequences from each of
186:     /// the child HIR expressions are combined via cross product.
187:     ///
188:     /// This short circuits once the cross product turns into a sequence
189:     /// containing only inexact literals.
190:     fn extract_concat<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a Hir>>(&self, it: I) -> TSeq {
191:         let mut seq = TSeq::singleton(self::Literal::exact(vec![]));
192:         let mut prev: Option<TSeq> = None;
193:         for hir in it {
194:             // If every element in the sequence is inexact, then a cross
195:             // product will always be a no-op. Thus, there is nothing else we
196:             // can add to it and can quit early. Note that this also includes
197:             // infinite sequences.
198:             if seq.is_inexact() {
199:                 // If a concatenation has an empty sequence anywhere, then
200:                 // it's impossible for the concatenantion to ever match. So we
201:                 // can just quit now.
202:                 if seq.is_empty() {
203:                     return seq;
204:                 }
205:                 if seq.is_really_good() {
206:                     return seq;
207:                 }
208:                 prev = Some(match prev {
209:                     None => seq,
210:                     Some(prev) => prev.choose(seq),
211:                 });
212:                 seq = TSeq::singleton(self::Literal::exact(vec![]));
213:                 seq.make_not_prefix();
214:             }
215:             // Note that 'cross' also dispatches based on whether we're
216:             // extracting prefixes or suffixes.
217:             seq = self.cross(seq, self.extract(hir));
218:         }
219:         if let Some(prev) = prev {
220:             prev.choose(seq)
221:         } else {
222:             seq
223:         }
224:     }
225: 
226:     /// Extract a sequence from the given alternation.
227:     ///
228:     /// This short circuits once the union turns into an infinite sequence.
229:     fn extract_alternation<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a Hir>>(
230:         &self,
231:         it: I,
232:     ) -> TSeq {
233:         let mut seq = TSeq::empty();
234:         for hir in it {
235:             // Once our 'seq' is infinite, every subsequent union
236:             // operation on it will itself always result in an
237:             // infinite sequence. Thus, it can never change and we can
238:             // short-circuit.
239:             if !seq.is_finite() {
240:                 break;
241:             }
242:             seq = self.union(seq, &mut self.extract(hir));
243:         }
244:         seq
245:     }
246: 
247:     /// Extract a sequence of literals from the given repetition. We do our
248:     /// best, Some examples:
249:     ///
250:     ///   'a*'    => [inexact(a), exact("")]
251:     ///   'a*?'   => [exact(""), inexact(a)]
252:     ///   'a+'    => [inexact(a)]
253:     ///   'a{3}'  => [exact(aaa)]
254:     ///   'a{3,5} => [inexact(aaa)]
255:     ///
256:     /// The key here really is making sure we get the 'inexact' vs 'exact'
257:     /// attributes correct on each of the literals we add. For example, the
258:     /// fact that 'a*' gives us an inexact 'a' and an exact empty string means
259:     /// that a regex like 'ab*c' will result in [inexact(ab), exact(ac)]
260:     /// literals being extracted, which might actually be a better prefilter
261:     /// than just 'a'.
262:     fn extract_repetition(&self, rep: &hir::Repetition) -> TSeq {
263:         let mut subseq = self.extract(&rep.sub);
264:         match *rep {
265:             hir::Repetition { min: 0, max, greedy, .. } => {
266:                 // When 'max=1', we can retain exactness, since 'a?' is
267:                 // equivalent to 'a|'. Similarly below, 'a??' is equivalent to
268:                 // '|a'.
269:                 if max != Some(1) {
270:                     subseq.make_inexact();
271:                 }
272:                 let mut empty = TSeq::singleton(Literal::exact(vec![]));
273:                 if !greedy {
274:                     std::mem::swap(&mut subseq, &mut empty);
275:                 }
276:                 self.union(subseq, &mut empty)
277:             }
278:             hir::Repetition { min, max: Some(max), .. } if min == max => {
279:                 assert!(min > 0); // handled above
280:                 let limit =
281:                     u32::try_from(self.limit_repeat).unwrap_or(u32::MAX);
282:                 let mut seq = TSeq::singleton(Literal::exact(vec![]));
283:                 for _ in 0..std::cmp::min(min, limit) {
284:                     if seq.is_inexact() {
285:                         break;
286:                     }
287:                     seq = self.cross(seq, subseq.clone());
288:                 }
289:                 if usize::try_from(min).is_err() || min > limit {
290:                     seq.make_inexact();
291:                 }
292:                 seq
293:             }
294:             hir::Repetition { min, max: Some(max), .. } if min < max => {
295:                 assert!(min > 0); // handled above
296:                 let limit =
297:                     u32::try_from(self.limit_repeat).unwrap_or(u32::MAX);
298:                 let mut seq = TSeq::singleton(Literal::exact(vec![]));
299:                 for _ in 0..std::cmp::min(min, limit) {
300:                     if seq.is_inexact() {
301:                         break;
302:                     }
303:                     seq = self.cross(seq, subseq.clone());
304:                 }
305:                 seq.make_inexact();
306:                 seq
307:             }
308:             hir::Repetition { .. } => {
309:                 subseq.make_inexact();
310:                 subseq
311:             }
312:         }
313:     }

315:     /// Convert the given Unicode class into a sequence of literals if the
316:     /// class is small enough. If the class is too big, return an infinite
317:     /// sequence.
318:     fn extract_class_unicode(&self, cls: &hir::ClassUnicode) -> TSeq {
319:         if self.class_over_limit_unicode(cls) {
320:             return TSeq::infinite();
321:         }
322:         let mut seq = TSeq::empty();
323:         for r in cls.iter() {
324:             for ch in r.start()..=r.end() {
325:                 seq.push(Literal::from(ch));
326:             }
327:         }
328:         self.enforce_literal_len(&mut seq);
329:         seq
330:     }

332:     /// Convert the given byte class into a sequence of literals if the class
333:     /// is small enough. If the class is too big, return an infinite sequence.
334:     fn extract_class_bytes(&self, cls: &hir::ClassBytes) -> TSeq {
335:         if self.class_over_limit_bytes(cls) {
336:             return TSeq::infinite();
337:         }
338:         let mut seq = TSeq::empty();
339:         for r in cls.iter() {
340:             for b in r.start()..=r.end() {
341:                 seq.push(Literal::from(b));
342:             }
343:         }
344:         self.enforce_literal_len(&mut seq);
345:         seq
346:     }

348:     /// Returns true if the given Unicode class exceeds the configured limits
349:     /// on this extractor.
350:     fn class_over_limit_unicode(&self, cls: &hir::ClassUnicode) -> bool {
351:         let mut count = 0;
352:         for r in cls.iter() {
353:             if count > self.limit_class {
354:                 return true;
355:             }
356:             count += r.len();
357:         }
358:         count > self.limit_class
359:     }
360: 
361:     /// Returns true if the given byte class exceeds the configured limits on
362:     /// this extractor.
363:     fn class_over_limit_bytes(&self, cls: &hir::ClassBytes) -> bool {
364:         let mut count = 0;
365:         for r in cls.iter() {
366:             if count > self.limit_class {
367:                 return true;
368:             }
369:             count += r.len();
370:         }
371:         count > self.limit_class
372:     }
373: 
374:     /// Compute the cross product of the two sequences if the result would be
375:     /// within configured limits. Otherwise, make `seq2` infinite and cross the
376:     /// infinite sequence with `seq1`.
377:     fn cross(&self, mut seq1: TSeq, mut seq2: TSeq) -> TSeq {
378:         if !seq2.prefix {
379:             return seq1.choose(seq2);
380:         }
381:         if seq1
382:             .max_cross_len(&seq2)
383:             .map_or(false, |len| len > self.limit_total)
384:         {
385:             seq2.make_infinite();
386:         }
387:         seq1.cross_forward(&mut seq2);
388:         assert!(seq1.len().map_or(true, |x| x <= self.limit_total));
389:         self.enforce_literal_len(&mut seq1);
390:         seq1
391:     }
392: 
393:     /// Union the two sequences if the result would be within configured
394:     /// limits. Otherwise, make `seq2` infinite and union the infinite sequence
395:     /// with `seq1`.
396:     fn union(&self, mut seq1: TSeq, seq2: &mut TSeq) -> TSeq {
397:         if seq1.max_union_len(seq2).map_or(false, |len| len > self.limit_total)
398:         {
399:             // We try to trim our literal sequences to see if we can make
400:             // room for more literals. The idea is that we'd rather trim down
401:             // literals already in our sequence if it means we can add a few
402:             // more and retain a finite sequence. Otherwise, we'll union with
403:             // an infinite sequence and that infects everything and effectively
404:             // stops literal extraction in its tracks.
405:             //
406:             // We do we keep 4 bytes here? Well, it's a bit of an abstraction
407:             // leakage. Downstream, the literals may wind up getting fed to
408:             // the Teddy algorithm, which supports searching literals up to
409:             // length 4. So that's why we pick that number here. Arguably this
410:             // should be a tuneable parameter, but it seems a little tricky to
411:             // describe. And I'm still unsure if this is the right way to go
412:             // about culling literal sequences.
413:             seq1.keep_first_bytes(4);
414:             seq2.keep_first_bytes(4);
415:             seq1.dedup();
416:             seq2.dedup();
417:             if seq1
418:                 .max_union_len(seq2)
419:                 .map_or(false, |len| len > self.limit_total)
420:             {
421:                 seq2.make_infinite();
422:             }
423:         }
424:         seq1.union(seq2);
425:         assert!(seq1.len().map_or(true, |x| x <= self.limit_total));
426:         seq1
427:     }

429:     /// Applies the literal length limit to the given sequence. If none of the
430:     /// literals in the sequence exceed the limit, then this is a no-op.
431:     fn enforce_literal_len(&self, seq: &mut TSeq) {
432:         seq.keep_first_bytes(self.limit_literal_len);
433:     }
434: }

582:     /// Compare the two sequences and return the one that is believed to be best
583:     /// according to a hodge podge of heuristics.
584:     fn choose(self, other: TSeq) -> TSeq {
585:         let (seq1, seq2) = (self, other);
586:         if !seq1.is_finite() {
587:             return seq2;
588:         } else if !seq2.is_finite() {
589:             return seq1;
590:         }
591:         if seq1.has_poisonous_literal() {
592:             return seq2;
593:         } else if seq2.has_poisonous_literal() {
594:             return seq1;
595:         }
596:         let Some(min1) = seq1.min_literal_len() else { return seq2 };
597:         let Some(min2) = seq2.min_literal_len() else { return seq1 };
598:         if min1 < min2 {
599:             return seq2;
600:         } else if min2 < min1 {
601:             return seq1;
602:         }

part.text:
Fixed. Summary:

**Root cause** (crates/regex/src/config.rs:433, `ConfiguredHIR::fast_find`): `--word-regexp` is implemented as `(?m:^|\W)(pat)(?m:\W|$)`. The fast path found the overall match and then stripped one character from each end, assuming both ends were real `\W` characters. But when `^`/`$` (zero-width line anchors) match mid-haystack (e.g. at the start of line 2 in `some.domain.com/x`), stripping ate a real word character, reporting `ome.domain.com` instead of `some.domain.com`.

**Fix**: decode the first and last characters of the candidate match and defer to the slower capture-group engine if either is a word character (meaning `^`/`$` matched rather than `\W`) — mirroring the upstream fix (BurntSushi/ripgrep commit `341a19e0`, #2574).

**Verification**: the issue repro now matches all three lines correctly with `-w`, and the full workspace test suite (758 tests, including all `-w`/word-matcher tests) passes with no regressions.
